The fibers in the mask material form a somewhat dense web. There are no straight paths through the material for particles to easily pass through. The N95 masks are not designed to keep all particles at the 0.3 micrometer (300 nanometer) range from getting through, but instead to block approximately 95% of particles that size. The mesh provides enough complex pathways to cause most of the particles to adhere to a fiber rather than make it through the material so you are effectively reducing the amount of particles you breathe in. They are not perfect and aren't intended to be. They are also not antiseptic/antiviral so it is purely a mechanical separator or filter instead of a germ killing barrier. You will definitely breathe in some infectious particles, but the mask will prevent you from taking in the vast majority of them. It's still a gamble but it does lessen your chance of casual exposure to the virus.

Adhesion at the small scale also matters. You know those vinyl decals that cling to glass? Imagine how well a particle could cling if it weighed a million trillion times less.

The individual virus particles have a coating of oil, which adds to their stickiness.
